Multivariate Regression

Beyond One Dimension
By setting a constant dummy feature x(0) = 1, the intercept b is 
absorbed into the weight vector as w(0). This simplifies the 
prediction equation. 
Absorbing the Bias
Can a the model fit a curve?

Polynomial Features
ONE INPUT, MANY FEATURES
AS A WEIGHT VECTOR

The Design Matrix
Squared Error
Same loss as before, now over four 
weights.
Normal Equations
Each power of x is just another 
column of X.

Choosing the Degree
Degree 1
Underfits: a straight line 
cannot bend.
Degree 4
Tracks the curve well, and is 
the most accurate model
Degree 3
Overfits: Tracks every point 
perfectly, with the lowest 
error, but generalises terribly.

Why Scale Features?
The Problem
For x between 0 and 10, x³ is 100 times larger 
than x. The error calculation is almost 100% 
dominated by 𝑥3. The algorithm completely 
ignores 𝑥 and 𝑥2, effectively throwing away 
those features.

Feature Scaling
Standardization
Mean 0, standard deviation 1. 
The usual default.
Min–Max
Squeezes each column 
into the range 0 to 1.
Rules of thumb:  scale x, x² and x³ separately, leave the column of 1s alone, and compute μ and σ on training 
data only, then reuse them at prediction time.

Scaled Gradient Descent
Unscaled
Learning rate must stay below 1.7×10−5. Loss 
is still 1.77 after 300 steps.
Standardized
A learning rate of 0.3 is stable. Loss is 0.83 
after 300 steps.

Key Takeaways
1
Add columns
Treat x, x² and x³ as separate 
features.
2
Solve as before
Use the normal equations or 
gradient descent on the 
design matrix X.
3
Scale first
Standardize each power of x, 
but not the bias column, so 
training is fast and stable.
